observations.flowers: melded instantly when received; some players omit flowers
observations.scoring: 10 or 20 for Out, then count pungs/kongs/pairs, then double

observations.scoring: point and double
observations.note: minimum 0, maximum 500
the oldest surviving variety, and the version introduced to America in the 1920s under various names; all players score and it is possible to score higher than the winner

sets out the point-and-double sequence in full and states that the Babcock system is derived from Chinese Classical scoring, which independently supports the chart's descent of Babcock rules from this node

chinese-classical.assessment: Four sources agree on the scoring structure and on all players scoring, and Sloperama's detail that a non-winner can outscore the winner is confirmed by Wikipedia. Wikipedia also independently derives the Babcock system from Chinese Classical, which supports the chart's placement of Babcock rules as a child of this node. The 136-versus-144 tile difference between sources is definitional: 136 is the wall, 144 the boxed set with flowers and seasons.

observations.scoring: count doubles, convert to points
observations.note: Sloperama's 'Hong Kong New Style': many many special hands, vs few in Old Style
wiki treats New Chapter as the transition from HKOS toward Guangdong style

CORROBORATES THE INTERMEDIATE NODE: states that HKOS was adopted as a backlash to HKNS, which had itself evolved from Chinese Classical, and that the simplified variant born from that backlash is Qing Zhang, Clear Chapter, known in English as Hong Kong Old Style. That places a new-style stage between Chinese Classical and HKOS, which is exactly what this node is

shanghai-hong-kong-new-style.assessment: The node's existence is now independently supported rather than inherited. Sloperama's Hong Kong New Style entry matches on tiles, hand and payout, and its 'many many special hands' against Old Style's 'few' is the substantive difference the branch depends on. The wiki's mainland page describes later pattern additions to the classical game as Shanghai New Style, and its GMCR page states outright that HKOS was adopted as a backlash to HKNS, which had evolved from Chinese Classical. Three sources therefore place a new-style stage between Chinese Classical and Hong Kong Old Style. What none of them does is date it to the 1920s.

observations.scoring: count doubles, convert to points
observations.note: few special hands; books: Perlmen & Chan, Constantino, Li, Lo, Tsui

observations.scoring: fan-laak; fan converted to points
observations.note: minimum and maximum both 'varies'; branched off traditional mahjong after WWII, prevalent among the upper class of Shanghai and Peking

observations.scoring: faan; common 3-faan minimum, 13-faan ceiling

observations.note: in the same table HKOS scores 0 similarity against 1920s standard Chinese Classical and 4 against the 1920s 'New Method', supporting the chart's decision to descend HKOS through an intermediate new-style node rather than directly from Chinese Classical

describes Hong Kong or Cantonese mahjong as differing from Chinese Classical in minor scoring details, and states it does not allow multiple players to win from a single discard, which is the opposite of the Taiwanese rule

hong-kong-old-style.assessment: Tiles, hand, scoring and payout agree across three sources. The date does not. The chart says fu was removed in the 1950s; the wiki's own Guangdong page dates the adoption of Clear Chapter, with pungs unscored and fu removed, to the 1970s; the wiki's HKOS page says only that HKOS branched off after the Second World War. The chart appears to have merged the post-war emergence of HKOS with the later Clear Chapter reform. Sloperama's early-forms table separately scores HKOS at 0 similarity to Chinese Classical, which supports descending it through a new-style intermediate.

observations.scoring: no standardised rubric; a popular variation is a minimum of three fan before winning
observations.note: wiki states the 3-fan minimum as a common variation, not a dated reform

observations.scoring: common 3-faan minimum and 13-faan ceiling
a winning hand must often reach some point value, anywhere between one and five points, with three being the most common
observations.note: presents the minimum as a player convention with a range, not as a dated reform

modern-hkos.assessment: Three sources now describe the minimum, and all three describe it as a convention rather than an event. Wikipedia's scoring article is the most explicit: the threshold ranges from one to five points, with three most common. The chart's 3-faan figure is well supported; its 1970s date is supported by nothing fetched here, and the wiki's own Guangdong timeline attaches the 1970s to the Clear Chapter reform instead.

observations.scoring: count doubles, convert to points
observations.note: books: Amy Lo, Dragon Chang

observations.scoring: pattern; unit tai; minimum 5 tai, maximum 300 tai

observations.hand: sixteen tiles, against thirteen in other versions
observations.note: features bonuses for dealers and recurring dealerships, and allows multiple players to win from a single discard. Separately notes that holding all eight flowers and seasons is an automatic win with a payout from all players

observations.scoring: linear, using tai (台), where the winning hand's tai count is multiplied by a factor and added to a base score
observations.note: contrasts this explicitly with the exponential doubling used in Hong Kong scoring

taiwanese-style.assessment: Four sources agree on the 144-tile set and the 16-tile hand, and two independently describe tai scoring as linear, which the wiki's infobox also shows. Wikipedia adds two structural features the chart omits and which distinguish the branch sharply from Hong Kong play: recurring dealerships, and multiple players winning from one discard. This is among the best-supported nodes in the tree.

observations.scoring: count points for hand characteristics
observations.note: discards placed in orderly rows

observations.scoring: pattern-based; minimum 8 points, no maximum
observations.note: length 16 hands; page shows a 2006 rulebook
mahjong certified as China's 255th sport in January 1998; unified rules codified that September

observations.flowers: eight, replaced from the back end of the wall
observations.scoring: 8-point minimum, enforced by a false-mahjong penalty
observations.note: the ruleset itself, confirming what the secondary sources say about it

TENSION WITHIN THE SAME WIKI: this page says that when there was a call to make mahjong a nationally recognised mindsport, the China State Sports Commission chose to eschew organic competitive mahjong and create MCR instead — a top-down invention. The wiki's Guangdong page says the opposite, that Guangdong Style was adapted into MCR and Zung Jung in the 1990s. The chart treats MCR as a sibling of Guangdong under HKOS, which matches neither account exactly

mcr-chinese-official.assessment: Sloperama and the wiki agree on 144 tiles, a 13-tile hand and pattern scoring; the wiki adds the 8-point minimum. Wikipedia independently dates the sport certification to January 1998 and the rules to that September, matching the chart. One wrinkle: the wiki's infobox is built on a 2006 rulebook, not the 1998 edition the chart cites.

observations.scoring: points-based; doubles built into the system

observations.tiles: 136 in 34 designs, four identical tiles of each
observations.flowers: none in the scoring system; bonus tiles noted as an optional addition some players make
observations.scoring: 44 patterns in categories and series, additive, with no basic points at all
observations.payout: only the winning hand is scored; the winner collects from the other three by a payoff scheme
observations.note: the designer's own official site, carrying version 3.3 of the system and his book Zung Jung: a Perspective of Mahjong History. It gives no creation date for the system
describes the general landscape of attempts at an international scoring standard, of which Zung Jung is one, and notes that most are not widely accepted

zung-jung.assessment: The rules are now primary-sourced: Alan Kwan's own site gives 136 tiles, a 13-tile hand, 44 additive patterns with no basic points, and winner-only payment, all matching Sloperama. That is the strongest evidence any node in this compendium has, because it comes from the system's designer. The date and the parentage remain open: the official site gives no creation date, so the chart's 2000s against the wiki's 1990s is still unresolved, as is whether Zung Jung descends from Guangdong Style or sits beside it.

observations.tiles: 108 (suit tiles only; no winds or dragons)
observations.payout: winner only; discarder pays for all
observations.note: Hunan: 5 ways out, hand must include a pair of 2s/5s/8s else seven pairs or pure. Tibetan & Sichuan: no more than two suits, punging OK, chowing not permitted

sichuan-hunan-tibetan.assessment: 108 suit-only tiles match. The source is more precise than the chart in a useful way: Hunan and Tibetan/Sichuan are given different winning conditions, so this single node covers at least two distinct games.

observations.note: Morten Andersen, newsgroup November 2007, on Sichuan style as played in Chengdu: kongs score very well; play continues after the first player goes out and does not stop until three players are mahjong or the wall runs out; penalty for holding all three suits at the end

observations.tiles: 108 across 3 suits, ranks 1-9, four copies each; no winds, dragons or flowers
observations.note: MIL 'Brief Introduction to Bloody Mahjong' fetched as PDF; blood-battle continuation and missing-suit requirement

observations.tiles: 108: any set with all honour tiles, flower tiles, red fives and jokers removed, leaving four each of 1-9 in three suits
observations.note: translates the name as Bloody Battle to the End. A chow cannot be called except for a winning hand, which is narrower than a flat no-chow rule

observations.tiles: 108 in three suits, Wan, Bing and Tiao
observations.scoring: tournament form caps the multiplier at three fan and adds game scores, explicitly to reduce luck
observations.note: describes Blood Battle as one of the most widely recognised and adopted mahjong rulesets within China, and states the one-missing-suit requirement

sichuan-bloody-rules.assessment: The best-evidenced node in the mainland group: five sources, four of them independent of the chart. All agree on 108 tiles with honours and flowers removed, the one-missing-suit requirement and the continuation of play after the first win. The wiki independently dates the Chengdu adoption to the 1990s, matching the chart. Two sources also qualify the no-chow rule: chows cannot be called from a discard except to complete a winning hand, which is narrower than a flat prohibition.

observations.hand: 7, out on 8 (some players hold 10, out on 11)
observations.scoring: unknown
observations.note: from conversations with author Dragon Chang; a very quick gambling game. Sloperama notes this contradicts the Chengdu account it also carries

sichuan-72-tile.assessment: 72 tiles, bams and dots only, a 7-tile hand winning on 8. Sloperama attributes it solely to Dragon Chang and itself flags that it differs from the other Sichuan account on the same page. The chart is right to carry it as a separate node rather than merging it.

observations.scoring: count the points
observations.note: from a newsgroup post by Jesse, May 28 and June 1-2 2003

CONTRADICTION WITHIN ONE SOURCE: the abbreviated overview describes Fuzhou as using no flower tiles, with honours treated like flowers as in the Filipino game and a Japanese dora-type tile as joker. That description matches the detailed FUJIAN entry, not the detailed Fuzhou entry, which says 132 tiles with one honour removed and no flowers or jokers

fuzhou-style.assessment: The detailed entry gives 132 tiles with one honour removed and no flowers or jokers. The abbreviated list on the same page describes Fuzhou as having honours treated like flowers and a dora-type joker, which is the detailed Fujian entry's description, not Fuzhou's. One of the two is contaminated, and there is no second source to break the tie.

observations.flowers: none; winds treated as flower tiles and replaced when acquired; a wild tile from the back of the wall serves as joker
observations.scoring: contributor Chris Jacques: 'The scoring system is beyond me'
observations.note: Sloperama separately records that Dragon Chang says a style similar to Filipino is played in Fuzhou (Fukien)

fujian-style.assessment: 124 tiles, winds as flowers and a wild tile as joker match the chart exactly. But it rests on one contributor who says openly that he does not understand the scoring, and the Fuzhou entry on the same page appears to have borrowed this description. Treat the tile count as the only firm part.

observations.flowers: unknown; the first picked tile dictates the wild tile, by similar logic to Japanese dora
observations.scoring: no minimum; 1 point per pung, 2 per kong (non-winners score for kongs too); kong doubles winner's score; only three special hands
observations.note: information from Laurent Mahe

observations.tiles: 136, three suits plus four winds and three dragons
observations.flowers: the eight flower tiles, four seasons and four flowers, are NOT used
observations.scoring: no open set or kong may contain a wild tile
observations.note: each player builds a wall 17 tiles wide and two high, which is 136 tiles across four walls, confirming the count arithmetically. The face-up tile is the wild indicator and the four tiles of the same suit one greater in number are wild; a nine makes the ones wild, a wind makes the next wind in East-South-West-North order wild, a dragon the next in Red-Green-White order. A wild tile substitutes for any tile in a winning hand

beijing-style.assessment: A second source settles what the first could not, and contradicts it. Sloperama assumed 144 tiles and recorded flower handling as unknown; the blog it cites states 136 tiles and that the eight flower and season tiles are not used, and its 17-wide two-high wall confirms 136 arithmetically. Prefer 136 and no flowers. The wild-tile mechanism the chart summarises as 'drawn wild tile' is corroborated and much more specific than either summary: the indicator is face up, and the wild tiles are the four one greater in number, wrapping from nine to one.

observations.flowers: in addition to the regular flowers/seasons, the dragon tiles are treated as flowers
observations.scoring: points for flowers, doubled for special ways of going out
observations.note: revealed by Shanghai player 'ithinc' on the mahjong newsgroup, 17-18 April 2006

observations.tiles: 144, of which TWENTY are flower tiles: four green dragons, four red dragons, four white dragons, the four seasons, and plum, orchid, bamboo and chrysanthemum
observations.scoring: flower scoring is the core mechanic, the flower count converted into points at a rate the table sets; kongs come in three kinds, exposed, concealed and flower kong, each scoring differently
observations.payout: a self-drawn win collects from all three opponents, while a player who discards the winning tile pays for one hand only
observations.note: also called Jinling Mahjong (金陵麻将), popular in the Nanjing area of Jiangsu. Winning hands divide into minor and major; four 'hard flowers', such as red or white dragons, are needed to qualify for a minor hand, and a concealed hand awards additional flowers. A major hand retains the dealership

nanjing-style.assessment: Two independent sources agree, and the second is far richer than the 2006 newsgroup report the node rested on. Both give 144 tiles and dragons treated as flowers; Baidu makes the arithmetic explicit, twenty flower tiles being the twelve dragons plus the eight seasons and plants. Both make flower count the scoring engine. Baidu adds the structure the chart lacks: minor and major hands, four hard flowers to qualify for a minor, a flower kong alongside exposed and concealed kongs, and a major hand retaining the dealership. The local name is Jinling Mahjong.

observations.hand: unknown whether 13 or 16 or another number
observations.scoring: unknown
observations.note: winning hand, if Sloper recalls correctly, must be PUNGS only (no chows); from conversations with author Dragon Chang

CONTRADICTION WITHIN ONE SOURCE: the abbreviated overview on the same page reads 'Shenzhen Style (played with KONGS - no pungs or chows - details not available at present)', while the detailed section reads 'Winning hand (if I recall correctly) must be PUNGS only (no chows)'. The chart follows the kongs wording

shenzhen-style.assessment: The source contradicts itself on the same page: the abbreviated list says the game is played with kongs and no pungs or chows, the detailed entry says the winning hand must be pungs only, hedged with 'if I recall correctly'. The chart follows the kongs wording without flagging the conflict. Tile count, hand size, flowers, scoring and payout are all recorded as unknown.

observations.scoring: points for characteristics of the hand
observations.note: revealed by Thierry Depaulis in a newsgroup post, 1 May 2006

macau-simplificado.assessment: 112 tiles and a 4-tile hand winning on 5 match the chart, and both the detailed entry and the abbreviated list agree. Its extreme hand size makes it the least mahjong-like entry in the tree that still carries a firm description.

observations.tiles: unknown; unknown whether flowers are used
observations.scoring: not clearly defined at maque.games; kongs may add points
observations.note: twelve ways of going out; more than one player can win; tip from Joe S., 16 January 2021
maque.games page reachable only through the Wayback Machine from this environment; brief English description

MEANING CONFLICT: gives 推倒胡 (tui dao hu) as the Mandarin term for a SCORELESS HAND, the Cantonese equivalent being 雞糊 (gai wu), in a passage about variants where scoreless hands are permitted. That is a general scoring term, not the name of a regional variant

tui-dao-hu.assessment: The name may not denote a variant at all. Wikipedia gives 推倒胡 as the ordinary Mandarin term for a scoreless or chicken hand, paired with Cantonese 雞糊, in a discussion of variants that allow such hands to win. Sloperama, working from the same maque.games page, guessed the meaning as 'push down hu' and recorded a variant with twelve ways of going out and multiple winners. Both can be true, since a ruleset can be named after the scoreless hand it permits, but the chart presents as a distinct regional style what at least one source treats as a common noun. Everything else about the node remains unknown: no tile count, no hand size, no scoring.

observations.tiles: 144 (some add 2 jokers for 146, probably a table rule)
observations.scoring: not reported
observations.note: fewer than 20 special hands; no chows; discards briefly shown then placed face down in orderly rows; drawn hands result in a goulash. Reported by Ian Stanley on the ReachMahjong forum, June 2009

chinese-casino-style.assessment: 144 tiles, no chows, and all players scoring. One forum report from 2009. The no-chows rule links it to the other chow-less variants, which is more interesting than the chart's bare label suggests.

observations.flowers: game requires 12 flowers: the 8 regular plus 4 animal flowers

observations.note: relatively few special hands; book: AMAZING MAHJONG by Celia Ching

observations.note: groups Singaporean and Malaysian mahjong together as sharing much with Hong Kong mahjong, and describes payouts midway through a hand when conditions such as a kong are met

singapore-style.assessment: Two independent sources agree on the animal tiles that define the variant, and Wikipedia names all four: cat, mouse, cockerel and centipede. Sloperama's 148 total and requirement of all twelve flowers is consistent with that. Wikipedia's mid-hand payout rule is a structural feature neither the chart nor Sloperama records.

observations.tiles: 84 (one suit, honours, 16 flowers, 4 jokers); a 108-tile variant also exists
observations.scoring: count the fan, convert to points
observations.payout: all players are paid, depending on what they hold
observations.note: Vincent Cheah describes the 84-tile three-player game
Sloperama's dedicated Malaysian page, fetched separately, covers the same 84-tile game
the abbreviated overview splits this into Malaysian 3-Player 'A' (84 tiles, one suit) and Malaysian 3-Player 'B' (108 tiles, details unknown). The chart carries only the 84-tile game

malaysian-3-player.assessment: The 84-tile one-suit game is confirmed with a full component breakdown. But Sloperama also records a second three-player Malaysian game of 108 tiles, which the chart does not carry at all, so the node covers only one of two documented forms.

observations.scoring: 50 points for Out, then points for pungs, kongs, pairs, flowers, then double
observations.payout: all players are paid, depending on what they hold
observations.note: winning hand must be All Chow, All Pung, or Half/Full Flush
Sloperama's dedicated Malaysian page covers the same 164-tile game

malaysian-4-player.assessment: 164 tiles and 24 flowers match exactly, from two Sloperama pages. The winning-hand restriction to All Chow, All Pung or a flush is a substantive rule the chart omits.

observations.tiles: 144 (possibly more); certain tiles may be designated as jokers
observations.flowers: melded instantly; winds and dragons are treated the same as flowers
observations.scoring: count doubles, convert to points
observations.note: kongs get paid at the instant they are melded

observations.hand: 16, and you must have 17 tiles to win
observations.note: cited by Sloperama's own catalogue. Confirms both the four plant flowers and the four season tiles, and describes a separate flower wall used for replacements

observations.flowers: groups all dragon, wind, season and flower tiles as flowers for bonus points
observations.note: states the game uses no jokers, which contradicts Sloperama's note that certain tiles may be designated as jokers under a rule it could not describe

filipino-style.assessment: Three sources agree on the 144-tile set and the 16-tile hand winning on 17. More importantly, Wikipedia independently confirms the flower handling that the chart's own new caveat makes the test for telling Filipino from Taiwanese: dragons and winds are grouped with the flowers. The one disagreement is jokers, which Sloperama hedges and Wikipedia denies; prefer Wikipedia, since Sloperama admits it cannot state the rule.

observations.tiles: version A: 144; version B: 112 (craks omitted except 1C, 5C, 9C)

observations.flowers: none in either; A has 8 red fives, B has 6 red fives
observations.scoring: A: 'simplified and streamlined'; B: count the points
observations.note: three-player game that originated in casinos in the Philippines, BASED ON JAPANESE MODERN AND FILIPINO RULES; version B reported by Vladimir, April 2015

bashi-bashi.assessment: Sloperama documents two incompatible games under this name: version A with 144 tiles and 8 red fives, version B with 112 tiles and 6 red fives, differing also on scoring and payout. The chart carries one undifferentiated node. Sloperama also says Bashi-Bashi is based on Japanese modern AND Filipino rules, while the chart descends it from Filipino alone.

observations.scoring: based on the 19 ways of going Out
observations.note: no books in English

observations.flowers: eight specialised jokers and eight extra flowers
observations.note: independently gives the same 160-tile total the chart and Sloperama give

vietnamese-classical.assessment: Two independent sources give 160 tiles built from eight jokers and eight extra flowers, matching the chart exactly. Sloperama adds the eight kings and queens and the nineteen ways of going out, which is the feature that ties the classical and modern forms together.

observations.flowers: flowers/seasons, 8 kings/queens, and 24 or more jokers
observations.scoring: based on the 19 ways of going Out

observations.note: describes the modern variant as triplicating or quadruplicating the jokers, which gives 176 or 184 rather than Sloperama's open-ended '176 or more'

vietnamese-modern.assessment: Two independent sources agree, and Wikipedia is the more precise: triplicating or quadruplicating the eight jokers gives exactly 176 or 184 tiles, where Sloperama says 176 or more and the chart says 176+. The mechanism explains the number rather than just reporting it.

observations.scoring: points for characteristics of the hand
observations.note: four threesomes only, no pair; threesomes are pungs and knitted pungs only, no chows. Book: Dobree, Gambling Games of Malaya, 1955. Existence revealed by Thierry Depaulis, newsgroup, 2 May 2006

pong-malaya.assessment: 120 tiles and the Dobree 1955 attribution match. The source adds the defining structure: four threesomes and no pair, pungs and knitted pungs only, an 11-tile hand winning on 12. That is a far more distinctive game than the chart's one-line entry suggests.

observations.flowers: come with the sets but are not used in play
observations.scoring: 20 for Out, then count pungs/kongs/pairs, then double
point and double; minimum 0, maximum 500
observations.note: dead wall 14, length 4 rounds

in 1929 the first organisation dedicated to mahjong players in Japan was established; the Federation still recognises Arushiiaru as its primary variant and accepted riichi as a second approved variant only in 2016

in Sloperama's early-forms table, Japanese Classical scores 8 (identical) against the 1920s 'New Method' column and only 4 against 1920s standard Chinese Classical, which places its descent through the new-style line rather than straight from Chinese Classical
dates mahjong's arrival in Japan to 1909, two decades before the 1929 organisation the chart uses to date this node
describes Japanese classical as closer to the Chinese classical scoring system but with only the winner scoring, and says it is still used in tournaments

japanese-classical-arushiiaru.assessment: Sloperama and the wiki agree on 136 tiles, a 13-tile hand and point-and-double scoring, and the Krakow Chombo Club history independently dates the first Japanese mahjong organisation to 1929. Sloperama's early-forms table adds real structural evidence: Japanese Classical scores identically with the 1920s New Method and only 4 against standard Chinese Classical.

observations.note: Amano Daizou published rules in the newspaper Houchi Shinbun between 11 November and 5 December 1952, for a game heavily based on tochuu riichi which he called simply riichi; the Houchi rules established the dora as the third tile from the edge of the dead wall. Amano then left the Federation and founded the Japanese Mahjong Association
independently states that the riichi variant played today emerged only after the publication of the Hochi rules in 1952, corroborating the Chombo Club account from a different source

independently confirms the 1952 Hochi Shinbun publication as the first standardised riichi rules, the report to the police by someone connected with the Mahjong Association of Japan, Amano's departure as its executive director, and his founding of the Japan Tile Association 日本牌棋院. Gives his dates as 1904-1982, which matches the other account's statement that the Federation accepted riichi in 2016, thirty-four years after his death

houchi-rules.assessment: Two independent sources agree that the 1952 Houchi/Hochi publication is the origin point of modern riichi. The Chombo Club gives the exact serialisation window, 11 November to 5 December 1952, and Amano Daizou as author; riichi.wiki, written by a different community, independently makes the same ruleset the hinge of the modern game. This is now one of the better-supported nodes in the Japanese branch.

observations.note: in 1957 Amano published 'All 1-Han Shibari', also known as the Tokyo rules

observations.scoring: a riichi bet costs 100 points; all tenbou are worth a tenth of their usual value and players start on 20,000; hands are graded kazumangan, shoumangan, hanemangan, daimangan and, for chuuren poutou, choumangan
observations.note: names the ruleset 東京ルール, also 全一飜縛り麻雀 (all iihan shibari), and dates it to 1957 with Daizo Amano as author. Crucially it states there is NO kandora and NO uradora in these rules, which is negative evidence that both arrived later. Its han-from-dice mechanic — each 1 or 6 rolled, or any pair summing to 7, adds a han, re-rolling until at least one is added — is the early variable form of what later became a flat bonus, and the page notes that this zoroba does not count towards the one-han minimum

tokyo-rules.assessment: Two independent sources now agree on the 1957 date, Amano's authorship and the one-han minimum that gives the node its name, and riichi.wiki supplies the Japanese titles, 東京ルール and 全一飜縛り麻雀. The page also settles a question the next node raises: the 1957 rules have no kandora and no uradora, so the chart is right to place ura dora at 1967. Its dice-driven han bonus is the early, variable ancestor of bazoro, and it explicitly does not count toward the minimum.

observations.note: in 1967 Amano published the 'modern rules' (gendai ruuru), introducing rounding fu up to the nearest ten, bazoro, oka and ura-dora, all still used today

states that the 1967 Modern rules introduced 2 HAN bazoro, oka and uradora. The '2 han' is the detail that reconciles this with the 1957 Tokyo rules, which already had a variable dice-driven zoroba: what 1967 introduced was the fixed two-han form still baked into modern scoring tables, not the idea itself

modern-rules.assessment: Two independent sources agree that the 1967 rules introduced bazoro, oka and ura dora, exactly as the chart says. There is an apparent conflict with the 1957 Tokyo rules, which already carry a zoroba, and it resolves cleanly: riichi.wiki specifies that 1967 introduced TWO HAN bazoro, the fixed form still built into modern scoring tables, where 1957 had a variable bonus rolled on the dice that did not count toward the minimum. The chart's attribution is correct once bazoro is read as the fixed form.

observations.flowers: come with the sets but are not used in play
observations.scoring: base points times fan; most easily scored from a memorised chart
observations.note: discards placed in orderly rows

observations.scoring: point and pattern; fu and han/yaku; minimum 1 yaku, maximum yakuman
observations.note: length 2 rounds, dead wall 14

observations.flowers: not used; modern sets come with four red five dora tiles, whose use is optional
observations.scoring: han from yaku and dora, plus fu from hand composition; at least one yaku required to win
observations.note: names the four-player game yonma (四麻) against the three-player sanma. Dates the modern riichi variant to the 1960s, with the explosion in popularity after 1969 and online play from Tenhou in 2007. It does not date red fives to 1970 as the chart does
standardised in Japan and South Korea, prevalent in video games, with riichi and dora as its unique highlights and discards arranged by order in front of each player

THE CHAIN IS INCOMPLETE: lists seven Amano rulesets — 1952 Hochi, 1957 Tokyo, 1958 Unified, 1963 Olympic, 1967 Modern, 1971 New modern, 1978 New hochi. The chart carries only the first, second and fifth. The chart's 1970 date for this node sits beside Amano's 1971 New modern rules, which it does not mention

modern-riichi-yonma.assessment: Three sources now agree on 136 tiles, a 13-tile hand and no flowers in play, and riichi.wiki adds the han-and-fu structure and the one-yaku minimum. The chart's 1970 date for red fives is still uncorroborated: riichi.wiki confirms red five dora exist and are optional but dates the modern variant only to the 1960s, with the popularity surge after 1969.

observations.note: names sanma as the three-player counterpart to yonma and says there is a well-established modified version of the rules for it, but treats it as an accommodation for when four players are not available rather than a separate lineage. The same page also describes two-player and five-player variations, which the chart does not carry
Sloperama's catalogue has no separate Sanma entry, so no tile count or hand size is attributed to the name
three-player variants are described in the Wikipedia article on Japanese mahjong

observations.tiles: a standard set with the north wind removed, 2 to 8 of bamboo removed and the four seasons removed, keeping the four flowers and no jokers
observations.note: states the three-player game is not a mere adaptation of the four-player game but has its own rules: chows cannot be melded from a discard, discards are placed in front of the player, and a player cannot win on a discard they themselves previously discarded, the sacred discard

sanma.assessment: Now properly sourced. Wikipedia gives the exact tile reduction and three rules of its own, and states explicitly that the three-player game is not a mere adaptation but has its own idiosyncrasies, which strengthens the chart's decision to give it a node. That cuts against riichi.wiki's framing of three-player play as an accommodation for a missing fourth. Both are describing real practice; the chart's node is better supported than the previous pass concluded.

observations.scoring: several regional systems, most commonly '1,5,10' and '1,3,6'
observations.note: Sloperama queries whether 104 applies only to the three-player game. Bamboo is absent from the listed suits, which is what the chart means by 'no bamboo'

observations.scoring: point-based; minimum 2 points, maximum 80 points
observations.note: length 32 hands, no dead wall

observations.flowers: uses season tiles but calls them flowers
observations.note: states that Korean mahjong does not allow melded, that is stolen, chows, and that Japanese mahjong is standardised in Japan and South Korea

sets out the Korean and Japanese three-player game: the north wind is removed, 2 to 8 of bamboo are removed, the four seasons are removed and the four flowers kept, with no jokers. That is a different reduction from the Korean 104-tile game, which drops bamboo entirely

korean-traditional.assessment: 104 tiles and a 13-tile hand are confirmed by two sources, and Sloperama's suit list independently confirms bamboo's absence, which is the chart's distinguishing detail. Wikipedia adds two rules that mark the branch: season tiles used but called flowers, and no melded chows. Note that the Korean three-player game described by Wikipedia keeps bamboo 1 and 9, so it is a different reduction from this node's 104-tile game. None of this establishes the parent, which is why the chart draws the link dashed.

observations.scoring: determine the total faan of the winning hand, then square it to arrive at the portion
observations.note: Sloperama states WMPA is Korean and BASED ON JAPANESE MODERN, which matches the chart's placement under Modern rules. Book: WORLD MAHJONG Essence, by Kingstone Kim

wmpa-wmf.assessment: 136 tiles, no flowers, and the distinctive squared-faan scoring. Sloperama states independently that WMPA is Korean and based on Japanese Modern, which is exactly the placement the chart gives it, under the Japanese branch but coloured Korean.

observations.flowers: if used, melded instantly upon receipt
observations.scoring: 20 for Out, then points for pungs and pairs, then double; kongs and flowers not used in Babcock's original simplified system
observations.note: fewer special hands than Chinese Classical; Babcock's opening line describes a set of 136 pieces
Babcock's 1920 translation, and the Parker Brothers / Milton Bradley licensing

Joseph Park Babcock, 1893 to 1949, born in Lafayette, Indiana. His Rules of Mah-Jongg, the red book, appeared in 1920 and was the English-language rule book; a second edition followed in 1923. He was also a member of the committee that published a standardised rule set

babcock-rules.assessment: Four sources agree on the 1920 red book and its role in introducing the game to the West, and Wikipedia adds the man, his dates and a 1923 second edition. Sloperama gives the rules themselves, including that kongs and flowers were dropped from Babcock's simplified system, and Wikipedia's scoring article independently derives the Babcock system from Chinese Classical, which supports the chart's descent. The 136-or-144 ambiguity traces to Babcock's own opening sentence describing a set of 136 pieces.

observations.flowers: used in the hand to form sets
observations.scoring: all sets earn points; the hand cannot go out until points reach at least 20; points can be doubled
observations.note: designed in 1924 by R.F. Foster to solve the Chinese Classical problem of high-scoring hands thwarted by cheap wins and frequent wall-building

twenty-point-mah-jong.assessment: 1924, R.F. Foster, and the 20-point minimum that gives the game its name all confirm the chart. Sloperama adds the motive and the verdict: Foster's attempt satisfied nobody but paved the way for American mah-jongg in the 1930s, which supports the chart's placement of it beside the American line rather than in it.

observations.tiles: 144 or more (jokers optional and variable in number)
observations.scoring: 20 for Out, then points for pongs/kongs/pairs, then double
observations.note: 70-80 special hands varying book to book; optional Charleston or Razzle exchange, and a Goulash after a drawn game. Sloperama calls this 'Vanilla Western' and suggests 'British Empire style' as the better name; played in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, India and Italy

PARENTAGE TENSION: calls Western classical a descendant of the version Babcock introduced, which matches the chart, but then says the term today largely refers to the Wright-Patterson rules used in the US military. The chart makes Wright-Patterson a child of this node rather than a synonym for it

western-british-empire-style.assessment: The rules are well attested by Sloperama and the descent from Babcock is independently confirmed. The relationship to Wright-Patterson is not: Wikipedia treats Western classical as largely meaning the Wright-Patterson rules today, while the chart makes Wright-Patterson one child among five. Sloperama's own naming discussion, preferring British Empire style precisely to separate it from American variants, suggests the chart's separation is the more careful reading, but the sources genuinely differ.

observations.tiles: 144 (some add 2 jokers for 146, probably a table rule)
observations.scoring: count points for pongs/kongs/pairs, then double
observations.note: 70-80 special hands; has a Charleston. Books: Wright-Patterson AFB OSC
Wright-Patterson origins among Air Force officers' spouses at Wright Field, Ohio; described as a distinct American approach played by military families

wright-patterson.assessment: Sloperama and The Mahjong Line agree on the Wright Field, Ohio origin among Air Force officers' spouses. Sloperama adds 144 tiles, 70 to 80 hands and a Charleston, which places it closer to Western than to NMJL American.

observations.scoring: count points for pungs/kongs etc., then double
observations.note: each round uses different rules: one permits chicken hands, another requires special hands, another is a goulash requiring all pungs in one suit, the fourth is dealer's choice with wild tiles; in some rounds a player can buy a discard. Sloper corrected his own earlier assumption that this was the same as British/Western after visiting Mumbai in March 2009

india-mumbai-style.assessment: The rotating round rules that distinguish this node are confirmed in detail, each round with different conditions. Notably the author records correcting his own earlier assumption that it was the same as British Western, after visiting Mumbai in 2009, which is a documented revision rather than an assertion.

observations.scoring: calculate points then apply doubles, with numbers varying greatly from other forms

observations.note: SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND: a targeted search for the Israeli Mah-Jongg Association's own rules, in English and in Hebrew (איגוד המהג'ונג הישראלי), returned nothing about the association, its rules, tiles or scoring. Results were dominated by American mahjong and general Jewish-mahjong material, which is a different subject. No second source for this node was located, and the association's own site was not found

israeli-mah-jongg-association.assessment: Still one source, and now known to be hard rather than merely unchecked. Sloperama gives 144 tiles or kards, a 13-tile hand, flowers melded on receipt, all players paid, and scoring whose numbers vary greatly from other forms — the last being the only real hint at what distinguishes it. A targeted search in English and Hebrew found nothing about the association's own rules; the results were swamped by American mahjong and general Jewish-mahjong material, which is a different subject and should not be mistaken for this node. Anyone with Hebrew and a route to the association itself would likely resolve this quickly; web search alone does not.

observations.scoring: 20 for Out, then points for pongs/kongs/pairs, then double
observations.note: similar to Western but with fewer tiles in the hand; this is what the chart means by an 11-tile winning hand

nepalese.assessment: 144 tiles with a 10-tile hand winning on 11 confirms the chart's 11-tile winning hand precisely, and the source identifies it as Western-like but with fewer tiles in hand, which supports its placement under the Western branch.

observations.note: records only that mah-jongg was adopted by British sailors who nicknamed it 'Bones' because the tiles were made of bone, and points to gunplot.net. It gives no tile count, no hand size and no scoring, and its claim is about the origin of the NAME rather than of the ruleset

observations.tiles: made by discarding the unwanted items from a shop-bought mahjong set: the dice and counting sticks are not used. Three suits of Minor Bones (Ricks, Balls, Sticks), four each of nine numbers, so 108; Major Bones being four Winds (East 'Eddie', South 'Sammy', West 'Wally', North 'Normie') and three Dragons (Red 'Blood', Green 'Cabbage', White 'Blanket'), four of each, so 28; and eight Pretties, four Flowers and four Seasons
observations.flowers: Pretties are declared when drawn and replaced from The Loose; each corresponds to a wind, so Plum and Spring belong to Eddie. A set of four is a Squint, both sets are Double Squints
observations.note: explicitly Royal Australian Navy: 'this is the way it was played in the Royal Australian Navy'. Sets with rounded bamboo backs are discouraged because they make unstable walls in heavy seas. The author, POETC Frank 'Choco' Munday, was taught in 1975 aboard Ibis by 'Bull' May, who had it from 'Knocker' White on Curlew, who had it from 'Windy' Hill on Queen Bee; he concludes the origins rest with no one individual, that the rules evolved from a standard form of mah jong, and that they were surprisingly standard across the fleet but never officially documented. The document was assembled by Gun Plot message board members

observations.scoring: a winning hand must reach a minimum of 50 points AND include at least one double aside from the double for tying up. East ('Eddie') takes an automatic double for being dealer and another for tying up. A concealed winning hand scores a bonus, as does taking the first Pretty, and the 'Do bone' off The Loose is an extra double
observations.payout: zero-sum: points are deducted from losers and added to winners, played at a cent a point, with the running scoresheet expected to total zero at all times
observations.note: NO CHOWS: a winning combination is four 'pairs' plus a 'double-up' — and in Pusser's jargon a 'pair' is three or four identical bones while a 'double-up' is two, which inverts the ordinary mahjong sense of the word. Named hand types are the Pure Hand (all one suit, worth three doubles), Majors and Moon. Played by three or four players; in the three-player game North sits out and the others build his wall. To draw is to 'pluck', to win is to 'tie up'

observations.tiles: three suits of Minor Bones with sailors' names for every rank — the Ricks (characters) running Jimmy Rick, 2, 3, Teeth, 5, 6, Lucky Rick, 8, Top Rick; the Balls (dots) running Bum Nut, Balls, Traffic Lights, Taxi, Spare Tyre, Jeep, Crane, Trolley Bus, All the Holes
observations.hand: fourteen bones in front of you to declare, having plucked the fourteenth — the 'Do bone', because it'll do — from the wall, the discards or the Loose
observations.scoring: points: tying up 20; a set of three 2 (minor, open), 4 (major open or minor concealed), 8 (major concealed); a set of four 8 (minor open), 16 (major open or minor concealed), 32 (major concealed); each Pretty 4; a pair of your own wind 2; a pair of dragons 2; plucking the last bone to tie up 2. Score = points x 2, then doubled once per double held, rounded to the nearest 100 and divided by 100 to give the cents each loser pays
observations.payout: each losing player pays the winner that many cents, and bonus points are deducted from the others and added to the winner separately
observations.note: DOUBLES: tying up, tying up as East, holding your own breeze, dragons, your own Seasons Pretty, your own Flower Pretty, and either the Do bone off the Loose or it being the last bone (one or the other, never both) each give one double; a Pure Hand and a Concealed Hand give three doubles each but forfeit the double for tying up. FIXED SCORES: Moon, 1s and 9s, and Winds and Dragons at 50 a bit, Big Lizard 30, Little Lizard 20. BONUSES: Squints (a set of four Pretties) 20, Double Squints (all eight) 50, First Pretty 10. PENALTIES: a 'shit tie up' — declaring under 50 or calling the Do bone in error — costs 50, as does East breaking his own wall

NAMED HANDS, defined: Moon is one of each Major bone with a double-up on any, Majors being winds, dragons and the 1s and 9s; 1s and 9s is four sets of 1s and 9s of any suit with a double-up on any; Winds and Dragons is four sets of those with a double-up on either; a Big Lizard is one of every tile of a single suit plus one of each of the four winds and a double-up of YOUR OWN wind, and a Little Lizard the same with the double-up on another wind. A Lizard is named for its suit, so a Rick Lizard, and a Big Rick Lizard when the player is South

PROCEDURE: the declaration is the call 'Do Bone!', which must come before the next player discards or it is too late; on hearing it every other player throws their bones into the centre, so the declaration cannot be walked back. Rotation: if East wins he stays East, otherwise East passes clockwise; the game also ends when the last bone leaves the wall, and East stays; a Round is complete when East has gone full circle. The book states its own terminology warning: a double-up is two identical bones used to complete a hand, while a double is what happens to the score

INDEPENDENT OF THE RULES AUTHOR: the main Mahjong article carries a sentence on the variant — a fast-moving variant developed by sailors in the Royal Australian Navy, using an alternative vocabulary such as Eddie, Sammy, Wally and Normie instead of East, South, West and North. It gives no rules, but it is a second hand asserting the Australian attribution. The same sentence appears in older mirrors of the article, so it has stood for some years

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION OF THE TRADITION: an RAN veterans' slang index, unconnected to the rules author, glosses 'Bones' as 'Mah-jongg tiles' outright. It also independently carries the register the guide is written in — 'grey funnel line' as ships of the Royal Australian Navy, 'roughers' as stormy weather, 'gash' as rubbish, 'macca' in its sweets sense. This corroborates that the game and its name are real RAN culture rather than one author's reconstruction. It says nothing about the rules

INCONSISTENCY WITH THE BOOK, ALL-OF: the website covers only one case of holding four identical bones — finding them while sorting, where the set must be declared, REMAIN CONCEALED and be placed face down. The book adds a second case the website does not have, All-Of (declared): if you have already declared a set of three and then pluck the fourth, you place it with your declared set. The book then contradicts itself, a later passage saying that plucking a fourth bone into a set means placing all four FACE DOWN

LEAD CLOSED, NOT INDEPENDENT: the thread is a single post linking to the Gun Plot site, with no account of play from anyone. It is not a second witness. This could not be read from here — Cloudflare, and no usable archive snapshot — so it is recorded as reported by the repository owner, who opened the page directly; it is the one item in this node not read at its source

THE SITE IS GONE. gunplot.net still resolves but the host serves a certificate for an unrelated name and no longer returns the guide. The Wayback Machine copies used here are the surviving form of the website, which makes the archive the primary route to it rather than a workaround

pussers-bones.assessment:
A complete ruleset is on record and the search for a second witness is now finished rather than merely unfinished. Every trail leads back to one man.

The numbers are stable across the two forms of his account: the points, doubles, fixed-score, bonus and penalty tables are word-for-word identical between the website and the book, as is the scoring procedure — points times two, doubled once per double, rounded to the nearest hundred, divided by a hundred, and that many cents from each loser. 98 sentences are identical. They are one document in two forms.

ONE MATERIAL DISCREPANCY, and it is a scoring one. On holding four identical bones, the website covers only the hand-sorting case: declare the set, keep it CONCEALED, place it face down. The book adds a case the website lacks — if a set of three has already been declared and the fourth is then plucked, it joins the declared, open set — and then contradicts itself, a later passage saying a fourth bone plucked into a set goes face down. The difference is worth double: a set of four minors scores 8 open against 16 concealed, majors 16 against 32.

The points table settles it. It lists open and concealed rows separately for sets of four, so if every four-of-a-kind were concealed the two open rows would be unreachable. The book's All-Of (declared) rule is operative, the website is incomplete rather than wrong, and the book's later face-down sentence is the error. Build from the book; keep the contradiction on the record.

WHY THIS STAYS ONE WITNESS. The BoardGameGeek thread, the last open lead, turns out to be a single post linking to the Gun Plot site: a pointer, not an account. The site itself is now gone — the domain resolves but serves a certificate for an unrelated host — so the Wayback copies are its surviving form. Wikipedia's sentence on the variant and an RAN veterans' slang glossary both stand outside the author's work, and together they establish that the game and its name are genuine Royal Australian Navy culture: the glossary, unconnected to him, glosses 'Bones' as 'Mah-jongg tiles' and carries his register — grey funnel line, roughers, gash. Neither corroborates a single rule. What is missing is not evidence that the tradition existed but a second person's account of how it was played, and the author predicted exactly this, writing that the origins rest with no one individual and that the rules were never officially documented.

A caution for anyone repeating the search: this repository's own pull requests now appear in web results for Pusser's Bones. They are not sources and must not be cited back into it.

COPYRIGHT: the book is © 2023 Hot Rod Handbooks, all rights reserved, and sells commercially; the Gun Plot site separately restricted reproduction of substantial parts. Mechanics are recorded here as facts, as tile counts are for every other variant. Neither text is reproduced and neither file is filed in this repository.

observations.note: records a 1924 'American Code of Laws for Mah-Jongg' produced by a committee of publishers and enthusiasts, which unified variations before the NMJL's 1937 standardisation
describes the proliferation of incompatible American rule sets before standardisation

records that Babcock himself sat on the committee that published a standardised rule set, which is the 1924 American Code of Laws that Grokipedia describes. The pre-NMJL standardisation effort therefore involved the man whose rules it was trying to supersede

regional-us-house-rules.assessment: Three sources support a distinct pre-NMJL layer: a 1924 American Code of Laws produced by a committee, the proliferation of incompatible rule sets that prompted it, and Babcock's own membership of that committee. The node is a real stage rather than a placeholder, though no source gives it tiles or a hand size because it is a period rather than a ruleset.

observations.note: in 1937 four women, Viola Cecil, Dorothy Meyerson, Herma Jacobs and Hortense Potter, founded the National Mah Jongg League in New York City; nearly 400 women rallied at Manhattan's Essex House hotel to support standardising American rules
dates the founding to 1937 in New York City, by a group of predominantly Jewish women from the Upper West Side
dates the founding to 1937 in New York City
dates the NMJL's start to 1937
CONFLICT: states that the National Mah Jongg League, Inc. published a volume of 'Official American Rules' in 1935, which predates the 1937 founding date the other four sources give
RESOLVES THE CONFLICT: the League's own site, selling the 2026 card, describes itself as celebrating 89 years. Counting back from 2026 gives 1937, which is the League's own dating of its founding

nmjl-card.assessment: The conflict is settled. Four secondary sources date the founding to 1937 in New York City, two of them naming the Essex House meeting, and the League's own website now confirms it from the inside: in 2026 it celebrates 89 years, which counts back to 1937. Wikipedia's statement that the League published Official American Rules in 1935 cannot be reconciled with that and should be treated as the outlier; whatever the 1935 publication was, the organisation dates itself from 1937.

observations.tiles: 152 (8 jokers added to a regular Chinese set)
observations.flowers: used in the hand; they can be punged and konged
observations.scoring: look it up on the card, available from NMJL and/or AMJA
observations.note: about 52 special hands, which players must make; no free-form hands; the card changes every year; has the Charleston. Sloperama notes the make-up of the American set fluctuated in the 1940s, 50s and 60s

observations.scoring: score card
observations.note: no dead wall
joker tiles were added to the official rules in 1961
jokers appear in sets from the 1940s, with the NMJL mandate from the 1960-61 season

uses joker tiles, the Charleston, melds of five or more tiles, treats bonus tiles as honours and eschews both the chow and the notion of a standard hand; permitted hands change annually through a card that must be purchased from one of the sponsoring bodies. Notes that purists claim this makes it a separate game

american-mah-jongg.assessment: Five sources. Tiles, hand and the annual card are agreed; Wikipedia adds the features that separate this branch structurally from every other node in the tree, melds of five or more and no chow at all. The joker date is consistent across sources at 1961 or the 1960-61 season. Nothing here records what is printed on any card, which is deliberate.

observations.note: the scorecard is published annually by both the National Mah Jongg League and the American Mah-Jongg Association; the AMJA card is the second of the two
describes the annual card as an artefact and how the NMJL and AMJA cards differ in form
the AMJA is named alongside the NMJL as one of the two bodies publishing an annual card, and the two are described as having minor scoring differences
not relevant to this node; recorded only to note that amja.net itself could not be read, its TLS certificate having expired, so no primary source for this node was obtainable

amja-card.assessment: Two sources confirm the AMJA card exists as the second of the two annual American cards and that the NMJL and AMJA differ in minor scoring details. The association's own site could not be read: amja.net serves an expired certificate, and it was not fetched over an unverified connection. So the node is attested but not primary-sourced, and no source read here describes how the two cards differ in practice.

observations.note: special two-handed rules by Gladys Grad, 2015; the name plays on 'Siamese twins'. Two players each play two hands on specially designed two-tiered racks. Primarily designed with American mah-jongg in mind, but the concept can be applied to any variant

the cited site was read through the Wayback Machine. The archived homepage is about Mah Jongg Master Points, American tournaments and prizes, and does not describe Siamese Mah Jongg at all, so the citation does not currently support the node's rules claims

siamese-mah-jongg.assessment: Sloperama gives the substance: Gladys Grad, 2015, two players each playing two hands on two-tiered racks, with the concept applicable to any variant. The chart's own canonical source for the node, mahjongg.org, does not corroborate it: its archived homepage is a tournament and Master Points site that does not mention Siamese Mah Jongg. The variant is attested, but by the other source, not the cited one.

observations.note: a form of play similar to usual international competition forms; the walls are prebuilt so as to remove the element of luck, making winning a matter of skill; designed so mahjong can be considered a mind sport and qualify as a potential Olympic event
the Mahjong International League's own rules page, fetched and confirmed to exist at the cited URL

MIL describes itself as operating under the International Mind Sports Association with member associations in more than 50 countries, states that it initiated the duplicate format to decrease luck, and calls it an innovation that sublimates mahjong from a game into a real mind sport. It recognises MCR, Riichi and Sichuan rules as the three main international competition rulesets

duplicate-mahjong.assessment: Three sources agree on the prebuilt walls and the mind-sport motive, and the organisation's own homepage confirms both the motive and the institutional context: MIL sits under the International Mind Sports Association with members in over 50 countries. A useful side finding: MIL names MCR, Riichi and Sichuan rules as the three main international competition rulesets, which independently marks how far Sichuan Bloody Rules has travelled beyond its region.

observations.flowers: optional; if used, melded instantly when received
observations.scoring: points for pongs/kongs/pairs, then an 'aux' value, then multiply
observations.note: several special hands

observations.flowers: does not use Flowers and Seasons at all
observations.scoring: retains point scoring for basic sets, as Japanese and classical rules do, rather than scoring only kongs as the Internet Mahjong Server rules do; a self-drawn win receives 10 AUXILIARY POINTS; patterns score slightly better concealed, and a fully concealed hand is rewarded
observations.note: DATES AND NAMES THE NODE: rules created for the 1997 Mahjong Masters Millions tournament by Zuwei Thomas Feng and Hiroyuki Takashaki. They are IMS (Internet Mahjong Server) rules — hybrid, combining features of modern Chinese and Japanese mahjong. Pattern selection resembles modern Japanese, with hands such as All Simples and Terminal or Honour in each set, but the Japanese low-scoring patterns are abandoned: no-points hand, going out on a pair, one-chance chow. It applies the Japanese sacred-discard rule in its extended form, and missed discard

mahjong-masters-millions.assessment:
Two sources, and the second turns a bare label into a dated, attributed ruleset: created for the 1997 Mahjong Masters Millions tournament by Zuwei Thomas Feng and Hiroyuki Takashaki, as Internet Mahjong Server rules — a deliberate hybrid of modern Chinese and Japanese play. Pattern selection follows the Japanese side, including the sacred-discard and missed-discard rules and better scoring for concealed hands, while the Japanese low-scoring patterns are dropped and a self-drawn win instead takes auxiliary points in the Chinese modern style.

It also decodes Sloperama. Its entry says to score the sets, then 'determine the aux value, then multiply' without saying what aux is; the preset documentation shows auxiliary points in use, ten of them for a self-drawn win. The one disagreement is flowers: Sloperama calls them optional and gives 136 or 144 tiles, while this source says the ruleset does not use flowers and seasons at all, which resolves the count to 136.

The chart's placement under modern inventions is well supported by this. A 1997 tournament ruleset assembled deliberately from two traditions is an invention, not a descendant.

observations.note: Sloperama's family tree page gives the Matiao / Khanhoo / dominoes root structure the chart's root node stands for
Stanwick and Xu's tile-set research on early ma que, underlying the Hua Maque and Wang Maque material

dates the physical evidence: the ma que pai sets of Carl Himly and George Glover were collected in 1868-1876, 1872-1873 and 1875, and the wind tiles are found in most known ma que pai sets after the 1870s. The game is 麻雀 ma que, literally 'hemp bird' and in bonded form 'sparrow', also known in the Late Qing period as peng hu, 'encountering harmony'

names the ancestry directly: khanhoo is a non-partnership draw-and-discard Chinese card game, first recorded in the late Ming as a multi-trick-taking game, which 'belongs to the same family as Mahjong'. By the late Qing the rules Wilkinson and Culin recorded had changed from trick-taking to draw-and-discard, a shift attributed to the 18th and 19th centuries when trick-taking gave way to shedding games — mòhú (默和) and pènghú (碰和), which it calls the ancestors of mahjong. Wilkinson had Charles Goodall issue a khanhoo pack with a rules booklet in 1891

proto-mahjong.assessment: Well dated, and now with a named mechanism of descent. Stanwick and Xu date surviving ma que pai sets to collections made between 1868 and 1876, with wind tiles in most known sets after the 1870s, which corroborates the chart's c. 1870s by artefacts rather than by rules. Wikipedia's khanhoo article supplies the structural story: the family shifted from trick-taking to draw-and-discard across the 18th and 19th centuries as shedding games — mòhú and pènghú, named there as mahjong's ancestors — displaced the older form. That is what this node stands for. The chart's other claim, that the rules are lost, no source contradicts: what survives from the period is tiles, cards and collectors' notes, not a ruleset.

observations.note: listed as 'Chinese Archaic (1890 rules per Wilkinson)', matching the chart's date and attribution

Sloperama's early-forms table compares 1903 (Li), 1915 (Mauger), 1920s standard, 1920s 'New Method', Japanese Classical and HKOS against eight rule hallmarks; Chinese Archaic itself is not a column in that table

the collector behind this node: Sir William Henry Wilkinson, British sinologist and Consul-General in China and Korea from 1880 to 1918. His packs were procured during 1889-90 from Guangzhou, Shantou and Fuzhou in the south, Ningbo and Shanghai on the coast, Beijing in the north, Jiujiang and Yichang in mid-China and Chongqing in the far west. The collection is now in the British Museum

CONFIRMS THE DATE FROM ARTEFACTS: the characters 中發 appear on a box of precursor má qiǎo TILES collected by Wilkinson in 1889, donated to the British Museum as part of the Schreiber Collection. So Wilkinson's 1889-90 material is not only cards — tiles survive and are datable. It also cites an unpublished Wilkinson memorandum of 1925

chinese-archaic.assessment:
The chart's 'c. 1890, Wilkinson' is now supported by three sources and, better, by surviving objects. Wilkinson collected across nine Chinese cities in 1889-90, and a box of precursor má qiǎo tiles he collected in 1889 is in the British Museum's Schreiber Collection with 中發 on it. The date is therefore artefactual rather than merely asserted.

One caution about what the node contains. Wilkinson's best-known documentation is of money-suited CARDS — khanhoo and kunpai — rather than of a tile-mahjong ruleset, and he adapted khanhoo for Western players in 1891. Tiles and cards both survive from his collecting, so the node is not misplaced, but a reader should not assume a written 1890 ruleset for tile mahjong lies behind it. What lies behind it is a collection and a scholar's notes.

observations.note: the 1903 (Li) column scores YES on the Chinese Classical hallmarks (10/20 for mahjong plus points for sets, count then double, concealed sets rewarded, East pays and gets double) and NO on discarder-pays-all, self-pick reward and settlement between non-winners. Its similarity score is 8 to itself, 6 to Mauger, 6 to Chinese Classical, and only 2 to HKOS
records that in the Late Qing period the game was also known as peng hu, 'encountering harmony', which is contemporaneous terminology for the period this node covers

late-qing-style.assessment: Sloperama's early-forms table puts numbers on this node. The 1903 Li column scores YES on all four Chinese Classical hallmarks and NO on the three new-style ones, and rates 6 similarity to Chinese Classical against only 2 to HKOS. That is independent structural support for placing Li 1903 on the ancestral side of the tree.

observations.note: listed as 'Chinese Pre-Classical (pre-WWI, source: Mauger 1915)', matching the chart
the 1915 (Mauger) column differs from 1903 (Li) on two hallmarks: East pays and gets double is NO, and settlement between non-winners is YES. Similarity 6 to Li, 6 to Chinese Classical, 2 to HKOS

chinese-pre-classical.assessment: The 1915 Mauger column differs from Li 1903 on exactly two hallmarks, and scores 6 against Chinese Classical and 2 against HKOS. Its position between Late Qing and Chinese Classical is supported by rule content, not just by date order.

observations.scoring: additive
observations.note: Guangdong Style (廣東十三張麻將) is described as popular in South China AND TAIWAN, based on HKOS but using a large number of 'New Style' winning conditions and an additive scoring system. Its timeline reads: 1970s, New Style became associated with gambling in HK and a 'back to basics' variant called Clear Chapter or HKOS was adopted, winning conditions shrunk and fu removed; 1980s, New Style conditions were added back and fan were removed in favour of an additive system, and Guangdong Style was born

although Guangdong is a mainland province, Guangdong New Style has more in common with variants coming out of Hong Kong, and Taiwan post-1990s; it never uses Joys or Treasure Tiles, almost always allows multiple winners on a discard, and almost always uses discarder-pays-all

guangdong-style.assessment: Two wiki pages agree that Guangdong Style is a 13-tile game built on HKOS with New Style winning conditions and additive scoring, born in the 1980s, matching the chart. Both also independently support the chart's caveat about influence running two ways: one calls it popular in South China and Taiwan, the other says it has more in common with Hong Kong, and with Taiwan post-1990s, than with its mainland neighbours.

observations.note: the same timeline ends: 2020s, the synthetic competitive variant Guangdong Mahjong Competition Rules (GMCR) is made. This corroborates the chart's 2020s date

observations.scoring: built only from rules found in historic Guangdong Style rulesets, and teachable as a three-step progression through Clear Chapter and New Chapter HKOS
observations.note: states GMCR was created to promote competitive Guangdong Style, with three goals: true to the game yet simple, easy to learn, and competitive — the last achieved by removing pure-luck wins such as Blessing of Heaven and the self-drawn win. Gives an explicit descent chain: GMCR evolved from Guangdong Style, which evolved from HKOS, which was adopted as a backlash to HKNS, which evolved from Chinese Classical
a tournament codification of Guangdong style, showing the parent variant in current competitive use

guangdong-mcr.assessment: The 2020s date is confirmed by two wiki pages, and the node is now substantive rather than a bare label: GMCR was assembled to make Guangdong Style competitive, drawing only on rules already present in historic Guangdong rulesets and stripping out pure-luck wins like Blessing of Heaven and the self-drawn win. Its own page also states the descent chain in words — GMCR from Guangdong Style, Guangdong from HKOS, HKOS adopted as a backlash to Hong Kong New Style, and that from Chinese Classical — which matches the chart's shape through this whole branch, including the intermediate new-style node.

observations.note: NOT FOUND. Neither Sloperama's catalogue nor any Mahjong Wiki page fetched here carries an entry for Hong Kong Taiwanese or HKT. The chart's node rests on the Sloperama catalogue as its canonical source, but the label does not appear there

observations.tiles: 144, the same set as 13-tile mahjong, including the eight flowers: the four seasons 春夏秋冬 and four plants 梅蘭菊竹; some players add jokers
observations.hand: 16, the sixteen-tile game of the Hong Kong and Macau region
observations.scoring: additive (加算法), because it has many fan types and many fan; contrasted explicitly with Guangdong mahjong, which multiplies because it has few patterns. Fan are unlimited
observations.note: MULTI-PARENT: describes the game as a blend (糅合) of Hong Kong mahjong, authentic Taiwanese mahjong, Japanese mahjong and MCR, with fan counts far larger than authentic Taiwanese, contrasted with traditional 13-tile Clear Chapter (清章) play. Locally it is simply called Taiwanese mahjong, 台灣牌 or 港式台牌. It has a ready declaration called ding (叮) which, unlike Japanese riichi, needs neither a concealed hand nor a stake, and pays a bonus for winning within one turn; and a carry-over stake mechanism called la (拉). The article carries a single-source reliability warning dated March 2023, and cites a Hong Kong Mahjong Association league rules PDF from 2020

hong-kong-taiwanese.assessment: No longer unsupported. Chinese Wikipedia carries a full article on 港式臺灣麻雀, the 16-tile game of Hong Kong and Macau, giving 144 tiles with eight flowers, a 16-tile hand, additive and unlimited fan, a ready declaration called ding and a carry-over stake called la, and citing a Hong Kong Mahjong Association league rules document. Two cautions. The article itself carries a single-source reliability warning, so it is one account rather than a consensus. And it contradicts the tree's shape: it describes the game as a blend of Hong Kong, authentic Taiwanese, Japanese and MCR rules, where the chart makes it simply a child of Taiwanese style. Its additive scoring is also the feature the article uses to contrast it with Guangdong, which the chart places on a different branch entirely.

observations.note: Sloperama catalogues the individual Southeast Asian variants but uses no grouping term 'Nanyang' and asserts no common parent for them
the wiki's family tree is the chart's stated source for this grouping; the chart itself draws the link dashed and states that no source establishes the descent

nanyang-variants.assessment: Sloperama catalogues each Southeast Asian variant separately and never groups them or asserts a common parent; the grouping term does not appear. This is consistent with the chart drawing the link dashed, and confirms that the grouping is an organising device rather than a sourced lineage.

observations.note: the World Mahjong Organization's English-edition Mahjong Competition Rules PDF was fetched successfully through the Wayback Machine (374 KB), confirming the cited document exists at the cited URL

observations.scoring: pattern-based, minimum 8 points, no maximum
observations.note: the wiki's MCR infobox names a 2006 rulebook rather than the 1998 edition the chart cites

observations.tiles: 144 pieces in total, of which 108 are numbered suit tiles across three suits
observations.flowers: one of each flower tile, eight in all; a drawn flower is exposed, declared 'hua', and replaced from the back end of the wall
observations.scoring: a hand worth less than 8 points is a false mahjong: the declarer forfeits 10 points to each of the other three players and may not win that hand
observations.note: read directly from the World Mahjong Organization's English-edition PDF. Its contents run from tenets and competition conduct through fan values, scoring, rankings, fouls and appeals

mcr-scoring-reference.assessment: Primary-sourced. The rulebook itself was fetched and read: 144 tiles of which 108 are suit tiles, a 13-tile hand, eight flowers replaced from the back of the wall, and an 8-point minimum enforced by a 10-point forfeit to each opponent for declaring below it. That matches the wiki's infobox and Sloperama's summary, and puts a number on the penalty neither of them gives.

observations.scoring: varies
observations.note: states there are over 100 variants of Mainland Mahjong today, but that as late as 1990 regional variants shared many rules; in the 1990s they began deviating, Sichuan/Chengdu added Bloody rules, some dropped Joys, some removed honours, some built on Old Style and some on an additive New Style. Chinese Classical is said to have been allegedly invented in Ningbo in the 1900s, with later pattern additions referred to as Shanghai New Style

mainland-regionals.assessment: The wiki independently confirms both of the chart's caveats about this group: over 100 variants today, and a 1990s divergence in which some built on Old Style and some on an additive New Style. It also dates the Sichuan/Chengdu Bloody rules to the 1990s, matching the chart's separate node.

observations.note: Sloperama lists Duplicate, Mhing, Siamese and Mahjong Masters Millions among its variants without grouping them; the grouping is the chart's own editorial device, not a sourced claim

modern-inventions.assessment: No source groups these as a category. Sloperama lists each of them among its variants without any shared heading. The grouping is the chart's own editorial device, which is exactly what the node label already admits.

observations.note: listed as 'Mhing (Suntex)', cross-referenced to Sloperama's Cards/Kards FAQ; added to the variant list on 17 November 2001. Attributing it to the publisher Suntex is more specific than the chart's bare 'card version'
dates the game to a 1982 publication by Suntex and calls it an abstract family card game based on mahjong. The article is an orphan and carries a single-source reliability warning

observations.tiles: the Spear's Games 1984 UK edition comprises 158 cards plus a rule leaflet, a scoring pad and six hand-reference tables, with six wild Mhing cards, six double-sided scoring cards and two blanks
observations.note: the deck is based on Chinese money-suited cards. Records the original release in the USA in 1982 by Suntex International of Pennsylvania, a company still trading in mathematical education software, and names its founder Robert Sun. Suntex did not operate outside the USA, so the game was licensed abroad, to Spear's Games in the UK

mhing.assessment: Three sources, and the node is now dated and attributed where the chart had only 'card version'. Wikipedia and a card collector's description agree on a 1982 Suntex release; the collector adds Robert Sun as the company's founder, Pennsylvania as its home, a Chinese money-suited card design, and a 1984 Spear's Games edition for the UK under licence. Card counts should be treated with care: the only count read at source is 158 for the Spear's edition including its extras, which is not necessarily the count of the playing deck.
